questions.title: Squared Odd Numbers
questions.objective: Filter and square odd integers in a single list comprehension.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read a line of integers and print the squares of the odd numbers, in their original order.
• Keep only the odd numbers. A number x is odd when x % 2 != 0 (this also works for negative numbers)
• Square each kept number
• Do the filtering and squaring in ONE list comprehension: [expression for x in nums if condition]
• If there are no odd numbers, print NONE

Example: for 1 2 3 4 5 the output is 1 9 25.

Given the integers, print the squares of the odd ones.
questions.input_format: A single line containing the integers, separated by single spaces.
questions.output_format: One line: the squares of the odd numbers in order, separated by single spaces, or NONE if there are no odd numbers.
hints: The filter part goes at the end of the comprehension: ... for x in nums if x % 2 != 0.
The expression part comes first: x * x.
An empty list counts as False, so if squares: ... else: print('NONE') handles the empty case.

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing the integers, separated by single spaces.
extra_fields.output_format: One line: the squares of the odd numbers in order, separated by single spaces, or NONE if there are no odd numbers.

questions.title: Enumerate with Custom Start
questions.objective: Number items from a custom starting index using enumerate().
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read a list of items and a starting number, and print the items as a numbered list.
• Each output line is the number, a dot, a space, then the item. For example 1. tea
• The first item gets the starting number, the next one gets the starting number + 1, and so on
• Use enumerate(items, start) to get the numbers. Do not use range(len(items)) or a manual counter
• Build the lines with a list comprehension and an f-string, then print them

Example: for the items tea milk and the start 5 the output is
5. tea
6. milk

Given the items and the start, print the numbered list.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the items, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the starting number (an integer).
hints: enumerate(items, start) gives pairs (number, item), with the first number equal to start.
Unpack each pair in the comprehension: [f'{i}. {item}' for i, item in enumerate(items, start)].
print('\n'.join(lines)) prints every line, or use a for loop.
questions.reference_solution:
items = input().split()
start = int(input())

lines = [f"{i}. {item}" for i, item in enumerate(items, start)]

for line in lines:
    print(line)

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: the items, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the starting number (an integer).

questions.title: Pair Lists with Zip
questions.objective: Pair equal-length lists of names and scores into a dictionary using zip().
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read a line of names and a line of scores, and pair them into a dictionary that maps each name to its score.
• The first name goes with the first score, the second name with the second score, and so on
• Use zip(names, scores) to walk through both lists together. Do not use indexes
• If a name appears more than once, the LAST score for that name wins (that is what assigning to a dict key does)
• Keys keep the order in which each name first appears
• Print the dictionary

Example: for the names Asha Ben and the scores 90 75 the output is {'Asha': 90, 'Ben': 75}.

Given the names and scores, print the dictionary.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the names, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the scores (integers), separated by single spaces. There are as many scores as names.
questions.output_format: One line: the dictionary printed as a Python dict, {name: score}.
hints: Convert the scores to ints first with a list comprehension.
dict(zip(names, scores)) turns the pairs into a dictionary in one step.
print(d) shows the dictionary in Python format.
questions.reference_solution:
names = input().split()
scores = [int(x) for x in input().split()]

name_to_score = dict(zip(names, scores))

print(name_to_score)

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: the names, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the scores (integers), separated by single spaces. There are as many scores as names.
extra_fields.output_format: One line: the dictionary printed as a Python dict, {name: score}.

questions.title: Map Sensor Float Conversions
questions.objective: Convert comma-separated tokens to rounded floats using map().
questions.problem_statement:
Task: A sensor sends its readings as one line of text, with the numbers separated by commas. Read the line and print the readings as floats rounded to 2 decimal places.
• Split the line on commas
• Tokens may have spaces around them. float() ignores spaces at the start and end, so ' 5.678' works
• Convert every token with map() and a lambda: round(float(token), 2)
• Turn the map object into a list with list(...), then print the values separated by spaces

Example: for 1.234, 5.678,9 the output is 1.23 5.68 9.0.

Given the line, print the rounded readings.
questions.input_format: A single line of numbers separated by commas (there may be spaces around each number).
questions.output_format: One line: the rounded floats, separated by single spaces.
questions.constraints:
1 <= number of tokens <= 1000
Every token is a valid number
hints: line.split(',') gives the tokens.
map(lambda t: round(float(t), 2), tokens) converts every token. map() is lazy, so wrap it in list().
Printing str() of a float gives Python's normal form, such as 9.0 or 1.23.
questions.reference_solution:
line = input()

tokens = line.split(",")
readings = list(map(lambda t: round(float(t), 2), tokens))

print(" ".join(str(x) for x in readings))

extra_fields.input_format: A single line of numbers separated by commas (there may be spaces around each number).
extra_fields.output_format: One line: the rounded floats, separated by single spaces.

questions.title: Filter Primes in List
questions.objective: Filter primes from integer list using filter() and a predicate.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read a line of integers and print the prime numbers among them, in their original order.
• A prime is a whole number greater than 1 whose only divisors are 1 and itself. So 0, 1 and negative numbers are not prime
• Write the test as a predicate: a lambda that returns True or False. It only needs to test divisors from 2 up to the square root of n, for example:
is_prime = lambda n: n > 1 and all(n % d != 0 for d in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1))
• Use filter(is_prime, nums) and turn the result into a list
• Repeated primes stay repeated
• If there are no primes, print NONE

Example: for 1 2 3 4 5 9 11 the output is 2 3 5 11.

Given the integers, print the primes.
questions.input_format: A single line containing the integers, separated by single spaces.
questions.output_format: One line: the primes in their original order separated by single spaces, or NONE.
hints: all(...) with a generator expression stops at the first divisor it finds.
n > 1 and all(...) is False straight away for 0, 1 and negative numbers, before any division.
filter(is_prime, nums) keeps the items where is_prime returns True. Pass is_prime without brackets.
questions.reference_solution:
nums = [int(x) for x in input().split()]

is_prime = lambda n: n > 1 and all(n % d != 0 for d in range(2, int(n ** 0.5) + 1))

primes = list(filter(is_prime, nums))

if primes:
    print(" ".join(str(x) for x in primes))
else:
    print("NONE")

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing the integers, separated by single spaces.
extra_fields.output_format: One line: the primes in their original order separated by single spaces, or NONE.

questions.title: Set Comprehension Clean Words
questions.objective: Extract unique stripped lowercase words using set comprehension.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read a list of words separated by commas, clean them, and print the different cleaned words.
• Clean a word by removing the spaces around it with strip() and converting it to lower case with lower()
• Skip words that are empty after stripping
• Build the result with ONE set comprehension: {expression for w in words if condition}. A set keeps each value only once, so Apple and ' apple ' become one item
• A set has no order, so print the words in alphabetical order (use sorted()), one per line
• If no word is left, print NONE

Example: for ' Apple,apple ,BANANA' the output is
apple
banana

Given the line, print the unique cleaned words.
questions.input_format: A single line of words separated by commas. Words may have spaces around them or inside them.
questions.output_format: One line per unique cleaned word, in alphabetical order, or NONE if there are none.
questions.constraints:
1 <= number of comma-separated parts <= 10^4
0 <= length of each part <= 50
hints: line.split(',') gives the raw words.
{w.strip().lower() for w in words if w.strip()} cleans the words and skips blank ones.
for word in sorted(clean): print(word) gives a fixed order.

extra_fields.input_format: A single line of words separated by commas. Words may have spaces around them or inside them.
extra_fields.output_format: One line per unique cleaned word, in alphabetical order, or NONE if there are none.

questions.title: Inverted Index Dict Comprehension
questions.objective: Map each unique character to list of appearance indices via dict comp.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read a string and build a dictionary that maps every different character to the list of positions where it appears. Then print the dictionary.
• Positions start at 0 and each list is in increasing order
• Keys are in the order each character first appears in the string
• Characters are case-sensitive, and spaces count as characters
• Build the dictionary with a dict comprehension whose values are list comprehensions using enumerate()

Example: for banana the output is {'b': [0], 'a': [1, 3, 5], 'n': [2, 4]}.

Given a string, print the index dictionary.
questions.input_format: A single line containing the string.
questions.output_format: One line: the dictionary printed as a Python dict, {character: list of indices}.
hints: The list for one character ch is [i for i, c in enumerate(s) if c == ch].
Use it as the value of a dict comprehension: {ch: ... for ch in s}.
A repeated character writes the same key again with the same list, and the key keeps its first position.

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing the string.
extra_fields.output_format: One line: the dictionary printed as a Python dict, {character: list of indices}.

questions.title: Nested Grid Generation
questions.objective: Generate N x M multiplication table matrix via nested list comprehension.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read n and m, build an n x m multiplication table as a list of lists, and print it row by row.
• Rows and columns are numbered from 1
• The item in row r and column c is r * c
• Build the table with ONE nested list comprehension: the outer comprehension makes the rows, the inner one makes the items of a row
• Print each row on its own line, items separated by spaces

Example: for 2 3 the output is
1 2 3
2 4 6

Given n and m, print the table.
questions.input_format: A single line containing two integers n and m.
questions.output_format: n lines, each with m integers separated by single spaces.
hints: One row r is [r * c for c in range(1, m + 1)].
Put that inside another comprehension: [[...] for r in range(1, n + 1)].
Print with for row in grid: print(' '.join(str(x) for x in row)).
questions.reference_solution:
n, m = map(int, input().split())

grid = [[r * c for c in range(1, m + 1)] for r in range(1, n + 1)]

for row in grid:
    print(" ".join(str(x) for x in row))

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing two integers n and m.
extra_fields.output_format: n lines, each with m integers separated by single spaces.

questions.title: Grid Replication Aliasing Trap
questions.objective: Contrast [[0]*n for _ in range(m)] against trap [[0]*n]*m.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: There are two ways that look alike for making a grid of zeros with m rows and n columns:
• safe = [[0] * n for _ in range(m)] runs [0] * n once per row, so every row is a NEW list
• trap = [[0] * n] * m makes ONE row list and repeats a reference to it m times, so every row is the SAME list

Read n and m and show the difference:
• Build safe and trap as above
• Set safe[0][0] = 1 and trap[0][0] = 1
• Print both grids with labels

In safe only the first row changes. In trap every row shows the 1, because all rows are one list.

Example: for 3 2 the output is
safe: [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]
trap: [[1, 0, 0], [1, 0, 0]]

Given n and m, print the two grids.
questions.input_format: A single line containing two integers n (columns) and m (rows).
questions.output_format:
Two lines:
safe: <safe grid as a Python list>
trap: <trap grid as a Python list>
hints: The _ in for _ in range(m) is a normal variable name that means 'not used'.
Multiplying a list of lists with * copies references, not lists. That is the trap.
print('safe:', safe) prints the label and the list with one space between them.
questions.reference_solution:
n, m = map(int, input().split())

safe = [[0] * n for _ in range(m)]   # m separate row lists
trap = [[0] * n] * m                 # one row list, referenced m times

safe[0][0] = 1
trap[0][0] = 1                       # shows up in every row

print("safe:", safe)
print("trap:", trap)

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing two integers n (columns) and m (rows).
extra_fields.output_format:
Two lines:
safe: <safe grid as a Python list>
trap: <trap grid as a Python list>

questions.title: Conditional Dict Filter
questions.objective: Filter pairs from dictionary where value exceeds threshold via dict comp.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read N key-value pairs into a dictionary and a threshold min_v. Print a new dictionary with only the pairs whose value is strictly greater than min_v.
• Equal to min_v is NOT enough: the value must be bigger
• Keep the original order of the keys
• Use a dict comprehension over d.items()
• If no pair is left, the result is an empty dictionary and prints as {}

Example: for the pairs a 5, b 12, c 9 and min_v = 8 the output is {'b': 12, 'c': 9}.

Given the pairs and min_v, print the filtered dictionary.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of pairs N.
Next N lines: a key and an integer value separated by a single space.
Last line: the integer min_v.
questions.output_format: One line: the filtered dictionary printed as a Python dict.
questions.constraints:
1 <= N <= 10^4
Keys are different words without spaces
-10^9 <= values, min_v <= 10^9
hints: Read the pairs with a loop: key, value = input().split(), then d[key] = int(value).
d.items() gives (key, value) pairs; unpack them with for k, v in d.items().
{k: v for k, v in d.items() if v > min_v}.

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: the number of pairs N.
Next N lines: a key and an integer value separated by a single space.
Last line: the integer min_v.
extra_fields.output_format: One line: the filtered dictionary printed as a Python dict.

questions.title: Any and All Predicate Validation
questions.objective: Validate metrics using short-circuiting all() and any().
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read a list of metric values and print three checks:
• all_valid: True if EVERY value is between 0 and 100 (both included)
• has_alert: True if ANY value is greater than 90
• has_negative: True if ANY value is below 0

Use all() and any() with generator expressions, such as all(0 <= x <= 100 for x in nums). They short-circuit: all() stops at the first False and any() stops at the first True.

Print the three results on one line, separated by spaces, in the order all_valid has_alert has_negative.

Example: for 10 50 120 the output is False True False.

Given the values, print the three checks.
questions.input_format: A single line containing the integers, separated by single spaces.
questions.output_format: One line: three words, each True or False: all_valid has_alert has_negative.
hints: A generator expression looks like a list comprehension with round brackets, and it can go straight inside all(...).
Python allows chained comparisons: 0 <= x <= 100.
print(all_valid, has_alert, has_negative) prints the three booleans with spaces between them.
questions.reference_solution:
nums = [int(x) for x in input().split()]

all_valid = all(0 <= x <= 100 for x in nums)
has_alert = any(x > 90 for x in nums)
has_negative = any(x < 0 for x in nums)

print(all_valid, has_alert, has_negative)

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing the integers, separated by single spaces.
extra_fields.output_format: One line: three words, each True or False: all_valid has_alert has_negative.

questions.title: Generator Expression Squares
questions.objective: Compute sum of squares of sequence lazily without storing full list.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read n and print 1^2 + 2^2 + ... + n^2.
• Use sum() with a generator expression: sum(i * i for i in range(1, n + 1))
• A generator expression makes the values one at a time, so no list of n numbers is ever stored in memory. A list comprehension inside sum([...]) would build the whole list first
• For n = 0 the sum is 0

Example: for 3 the output is 14 (1 + 4 + 9).

Given n, print the sum of squares.
questions.input_format: A single line containing the integer n.
questions.output_format: One integer: the sum of the squares from 1 to n.
hints: range(1, n + 1) gives 1, 2, ..., n.
When a generator expression is the only argument of a function, you do not need extra brackets: sum(i * i for i in ...).
sum() of an empty sequence is 0, so n = 0 needs no special case.
questions.reference_solution:
n = int(input())

total = sum(i * i for i in range(1, n + 1))

print(total)

extra_fields.input_format: A single line containing the integer n.
extra_fields.output_format: One integer: the sum of the squares from 1 to n.

questions.title: Multi-Key Lambda Sorting
questions.objective: Sort user dictionaries by multiple keys (age desc, name asc) via sorted(key=).
questions.problem_statement:
Task: Read N users. Store each user as a dictionary {'name': name, 'age': age}, then print the users sorted:
• Older users first (age descending)
• Users with the same age are sorted by name in alphabetical order (name ascending). Capital letters come before small letters
• Use sorted() with a lambda that returns a tuple: key=lambda u: (-u['age'], u['name'])

Example: for the users Ben 30, Amy 30, Cal 25 the output is
Amy 30
Ben 30
Cal 25

Given the users, print them in sorted order.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the number of users N.
Next N lines: a name and an age separated by a single space.
questions.output_format: N lines: name age, in sorted order.
questions.constraints:
1 <= N <= 10^4
Names have no spaces
0 <= age <= 150
hints: Build the list with users.append({'name': name, 'age': int(age)}).
Tuples are compared item by item: first -age, then name. The minus sign turns the age order around.
Print with print(u['name'], u['age']) for every user in the sorted list.
questions.reference_solution:
n = int(input())

users = []
for _ in range(n):
    name, age = input().split()
    users.append({"name": name, "age": int(age)})

ordered = sorted(users, key=lambda u: (-u["age"], u["name"]))

for u in ordered:
    print(u["name"], u["age"])

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: the number of users N.
Next N lines: a name and an age separated by a single space.
extra_fields.output_format: N lines: name age, in sorted order.

questions.title: Filtered Cartesian Product
questions.objective: Generate (x, y) where x + y == target via multi-variable comprehension.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: The Cartesian product of xs and ys is every pair (x, y) with x from xs and y from ys. Read xs, ys and a target t, and print only the pairs with x + y == t.
• Build the pairs with ONE list comprehension with two for clauses and an if clause
• The order follows the loops: for each x in xs (in order), go through every y in ys (in order)
• Repeated values in xs or ys give repeated pairs
• Print each pair as a tuple on its own line, such as (2, 5)
• If no pair matches, print NONE

Example: for xs = 1 2 3, ys = 4 5 and t = 7 the output is
(2, 5)
(3, 4)

Given xs, ys and t, print the matching pairs.
questions.input_format:
Line 1: the integers of xs, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the integers of ys, separated by single spaces.
Line 3: the target t.
questions.output_format: One line per matching pair, printed as a Python tuple (x, y), or NONE if there are none.
hints: Two for clauses in one comprehension work like nested loops: the first for is the outer loop.
[(x, y) for x in xs for y in ys if x + y == t].
print(pair) prints a tuple in the (x, y) form.

extra_fields.input_format:
Line 1: the integers of xs, separated by single spaces.
Line 2: the integers of ys, separated by single spaces.
Line 3: the target t.
extra_fields.output_format: One line per matching pair, printed as a Python tuple (x, y), or NONE if there are none.

questions.title: Nested Record Extraction
questions.objective: Transform and filter deeply nested JSON student records via comprehension.
questions.problem_statement:
Task: School data often arrives as nested JSON: a school has classes, each class has students, and each student has a list of grades. Read one line of JSON and print the honor-roll students.

The data looks like {"school": "GHS", "classes": [{"name": "10A", "students": [{"name": "Asha", "grades": [95, 90]}]}]}.

• A student is on the honor roll when the average of their grades is at least 90
• Skip students with an empty grades list (they have no average)
• Round the average with round(avg, 1)
• Keep the order of the data: classes in order, and students in order inside each class
• Build the list of (class_name, student_name, average) tuples with ONE list comprehension with two for clauses (classes, then students) and an if clause
• Print one student per line as: class_name student_name average
• If nobody is on the honor roll, print NONE

Example: for the class 10A with Asha [95, 90] and Ben [70, 80], the output is 10A Asha 92.5.

Given the JSON line, print the honor roll.
questions.input_format: A single line of JSON. Read it with json.loads(input()) after import json.
questions.output_format: One line per honor-roll student: <class name> <student name> <average>, or NONE.
questions.constraints:
0 <= number of classes <= 100
0 <= students per class <= 100
0 <= grades per student <= 50
0 <= each grade <= 100
Names have no spaces
hints: json.loads turns the JSON text into Python dicts and lists.
The two loops are for cls in data['classes'] for st in cls['students']. Put st['grades'] first in the condition so the and stops before dividing by zero.
Unpack each tuple when printing: for class_name, name, avg in honor: print(class_name, name, avg).

extra_fields.input_format: A single line of JSON. Read it with json.loads(input()) after import json.
extra_fields.output_format: One line per honor-roll student: <class name> <student name> <average>, or NONE.
